title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | C3 Vs Modern (Saragossa) | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Against the Modern, we want a sound positional line rather than a sharp theoretical race.
c3 is the quiet, strong choice: the pawns on c3, d4, and e4 lock into a chain so the fianchettoed g7-bishop bites on granite.
moves.teaches: A c3-d4-e4 chain neutralizes the long-diagonal bishop before it ever gets going.

moves.spoken: The bishop tucks into d3, where it defends the e4-pawn while the pawn chain looks after d4 — every unit covers the next.
moves.teaches: Build a self-supporting structure: pawns hold one square, a piece holds the other.

moves.spoken: We could play h3 to rule out a pin with Bg4, but Bg5 is the more aggressive continuation, provoking a decision.
With e5 the game sharpens — the idea is exd4 followed by g5 and g4, chasing the f3-knight off the defense of the d-pawn.
moves.plans: Meet the coming ...g5-g4 by resolving the centre before the knight is kicked.

moves.spoken: So we take on e5, keeping the h4-bishop passive rather than letting Black free it with the pawn break.
After the trades the question is the queen's-knight: Nd2 would drop the d3-bishop to Qxd3, so that square is off-limits.
moves.teaches: Before choosing a developing square, check that it doesn't undefend a piece behind it.

moves.spoken: Na3 looks ugly, but it's only a transit stop — the knight is bad on a3 for exactly one move, then it reroutes to its ideal square c4.
moves.teaches: A knight on the rim is fine if the rim is a layover, not a destination.

moves.spoken: Nc4 leans on e5. You might ask why, since the queen guards the pawn — but pressure isn't only about winning material; it ties the defender down.
moves.teaches: Attacking a defended point still pays: it pins the guard in place.

moves.spoken: f4 is risky and does loosen our king, but the logic is clean: if Black takes, we push e5 and win the pinned f6-knight; if he plays g5, we take the knight with tempo on the queen. Even the Qc5-check has an answer — an interposition that hits the queen — which is exactly the resource f4 was counting on. Remember the three ways to meet a check: capture the checker, move the king, or block.
moves.teaches: The three replies to a check are capture, king-move, and interpose — the block is the one people forget.

moves.spoken: Now recapturing with the pawn is tempting because it hits the f6-knight, but a move isn't good just because it makes a threat: Black slides the knight to d7, and the e5-pawn, hit three times, simply falls.
moves.teaches: A move that only creates a threat can still be bad if the threat is easily met and leaves a weakness.

moves.spoken: So Nxe5 instead — it makes no threat, but it banks the extra pawn cleanly and keeps our structure sound.
moves.teaches: The unflashy recapture that keeps the material and the structure beats the noisy one that gives them back.

moves.spoken: Two ideas carry the position. First, sidestep the coming Rd8 pin with Qe2 before it lands — even at the cost of the usual 'defend with the least valuable piece' rule. Second, prepare slowly and attack fast: overprotect the centre first, and once Black's king is loose, look immediately for captures near it — that's how a shot like Nxf7 appears.
moves.teaches: When the enemy king is weak, start your search with captures on its doorstep.

moves.spoken: The takeaway of the whole game: when a committal pawn move like g5 is played, stop and ask which squares it just weakened. g5 concedes f5, and a knight is the default piece to plant on such an outpost.
moves.teaches: After any committal pawn push, name the square it weakened and the piece that belongs there.
